title: The Second Door
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: The listing had said one bedroom. It had shown one bedroom, one bathroom, one kitchen, one sitting room. Mateus Ferreira had walked through the flat on his first evening and had counted them. In the small hallway, between the bathroom door and the bedroom door, was a third door. He had reached out and had, without thinking, turned the handle. It had opened.

chapters.title: The Extra Door
chapters.body:
The listing had said one bedroom.

Mateus Ferreira was thirty-one, and he had, that autumn, moved to Porto for a job in the small research group at the university that had recruited him out of his postdoctoral position in Lisbon. He had, in the three weeks before the move, looked at seventeen apartments online, and had settled on the one at Rua da Alegria three-eight-two because it was, of the seventeen, the one that had come closest to what he had wanted — a small quiet flat in a building that had been recently renovated but had not lost its bones, on a street with good light and low traffic, above a small bakery that opened at six in the morning and closed at three in the afternoon.

He had signed the lease over email. He had paid the first two months' rent by transfer. He had received the keys, on his first Friday in the city, from a small tired real estate agent who had let him into the building and had walked him to the second floor and had, at the door of the apartment, handed him the keys and had told him that if anything did not work he should call the number on the small card she had given him.

He had, that first evening, taken his suitcase into the apartment and had walked slowly through it.

The apartment had been small.

It had been, from the front door, one narrow hallway that ran the length of the flat, with a sitting room at the end. Off the hallway, on the right, had been a small kitchen. Off the hallway, on the left, had been the bathroom, and beyond the bathroom, the bedroom. The bedroom had had, to his relief, a good north-facing window and a small radiator that had, when he had turned it on, produced the low pleasant hum of central heating.

The flat had, on the whole, been exactly what he had signed a lease for.

It had had, however, one detail the listing had not mentioned.

Between the bathroom door and the bedroom door, on the same left-hand wall of the hallway, was a third door.

He had noticed it as he had walked back down the hallway from the sitting room. He had, on the walk in, been carrying his suitcase and had been looking mostly at the sitting room. On the walk back — with the suitcase set down and his coat off — he had noticed the third door.

It was a plain door. It was the same white paint as the other two. It had the same small brass handle. It had, along its top, the same small line of moulding.

Mateus had stood in the small hallway and had looked at it.

He had, standing there, tried to fit the door into what he knew about the apartment.

The apartment was, he thought, on the second floor of a five-story building. The building was a converted townhouse. Each floor was, according to the small floor plan the real estate agent had shown him during the video walk-through in September, a single flat. The floor plan had shown one bedroom, one bathroom, one kitchen, and one sitting room, arranged more or less as he had just walked through them.

The floor plan had not shown a third door.

He had reached out. He had, without particular consideration, tried the handle.

The handle had turned.

The door had opened.

—

Behind the door had been a small room.

It had been perhaps two meters by two and a half. It had had a single small window on its far wall — a narrow window, higher than a person's head, letting in the specific pale blue light of a Porto evening. It had had a wooden floor, of the same dark walnut as the rest of the flat, that appeared to have been recently swept. It had, on its right-hand wall, a small radiator, ticking faintly.

It had been empty.

Mateus had stood in the doorway.

He had, for a moment, been aware of a specific small sensation in his chest — the low careful sensation of a man who had just, in his own apartment, discovered a room he had not been told about.

He had thought: *it is a storage room. It is a small storage room that was not on the plan.*

He had thought: *the agent forgot to mention it. It is a bonus.*

He had stepped inside.

The room had been, on entry, exactly what it had appeared to be — a small empty room with a radiator and a high narrow window. There had been no other doors. There had been no cupboards. There had been no interior features of any kind. It had been, so far as he could tell, a small empty rectangle of interior space.

He had walked to the window. He had looked out.

He had seen the small courtyard behind the building. He had seen, three floors below, the small clutter of laundry lines and rubbish bins that any Porto courtyard had. He had seen, on the far side of the courtyard, the back of the building on the next street over.

He had, orienting himself, understood that the small room was on the courtyard side of the flat. It was between the bathroom and the bedroom in the hallway, but on the *outside* of the building — its window was on the same wall as the bedroom window.

He had turned and looked at the doorway from inside the room.

He had seen his own hallway.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man performing a measurement without instruments, walked back into the hallway. He had walked the length of the hallway from the front door to the sitting room, counting his steps. He had walked back. He had counted the space between the bathroom door and the bedroom door.

The space between the bathroom door and the bedroom door, on the hallway side, had been approximately two paces. Perhaps two meters.

The room he had just walked into had been about two and a half meters deep from the doorway to the window.

The building was not two and a half meters deep in that section. It was, according to his measurement, two meters deep.

He had stood in the hallway for a long moment.

He had then, with the specific quietness of a man not yet permitting himself to have thought what he had begun to think, closed the door of the small room.

The door had closed with a small ordinary click.

He had walked back into the sitting room.

He had, in the sitting room, opened his laptop, and had, on the real estate agent's site, pulled up the original listing for the apartment. He had, in the listing, looked at the floor plan.

The floor plan had shown one bathroom, one bedroom, one kitchen, one sitting room. The wall between the bathroom and the bedroom had been shown as a single unbroken line, with no third door indicated on it.

He had looked at the floor plan for a long time.

He had, at last, closed the laptop.

He had gone back to the hallway.

He had opened the third door again.

—

The small room had been, on the second opening, exactly as he had left it. Empty, quiet, dimly lit. The radiator had ticked. The window had shown the courtyard.

He had closed the door.

He had opened it again.

The room had been there again.

He had done this perhaps six or seven times, standing in his own hallway on his first Friday evening in Porto, opening and closing a door he had not known his flat had, and finding, each time, that the door led into a small room the building's exterior did not have space for.

He had, in the end, stopped opening the door.

He had, in the small careful voice of a man making a decision he did not know he was making, said, aloud in the empty hallway: *I will think about this tomorrow.*

He had gone into the bedroom. He had unpacked what he needed for the night. He had, at nine, walked out to the small restaurant on the corner that the agent had recommended, and had eaten a small meal, and had come home, and had gone to bed.

He had, in bed, lain awake for perhaps an hour.

He had heard, at one point in that hour — quite distinctly, from the small empty room he had discovered — a small clear sound.

The sound had been of a single footstep. It had been the sound of a single soft footstep on a wooden floor, in the specific small way of a person stepping once and then standing still.

He had lain very still.

He had waited.

There had been no second footstep.

There had been, in fact, no further sound. The room, so far as he could tell in the specific total silence of a Porto flat at eleven-thirty at night, had gone back to being empty.

He had, at last, gotten up.

He had walked into the hallway.

He had stood at the door of the small room.

He had, after a very long moment, put his hand on the handle.

He had turned it.

He had opened the door.

The small room had been empty.

He had shone the light of his phone into it. He had seen no one. He had, in the specific small way of a man doing something he did not entirely believe he was doing, walked into the room and had checked its four corners. He had checked behind the door. He had, feeling foolish and also not foolish, looked up at the ceiling.

The room had been empty.

He had come out.

He had closed the door.

He had, standing in the hallway in his pyjamas at midnight, said aloud: *there is nothing there.*

He had gone back to bed.

He had, that night, eventually slept.

chapters.title: What the Door Was For
chapters.body:
He tried, over the first week, not to open it.

He did this in the small careful way of a man rationing an obsession. He had, on the Saturday morning after the first night, gotten up and had gone about his ordinary business — coffee, breakfast, a walk to the bakery below and back with a small paper bag of pastel de nata — and had, on returning to the flat, walked past the third door without opening it. He had gone into the sitting room. He had set up his laptop on the small table. He had, for the whole of Saturday morning, worked on a paper he had been meaning to finish for six weeks.

He had opened the door at eleven-fifteen.

He had done this without meaning to. He had gotten up from the sitting room to make a second coffee, and had walked into the hallway, and had, in the small unconscious way of a man passing a bookshelf and reaching out to touch a book, put his hand on the handle of the third door as he had walked past it, and had turned it.

The room had been empty. It had been, in the small brighter light of a Saturday morning, quite ordinary. The radiator had been ticking. The window had shown the small courtyard.

He had closed the door.

He had made his coffee.

He had, at three that afternoon, opened it again.

He had, over the course of that Saturday, opened it seven times. He had, on the Sunday, opened it twelve times. He had, on the Monday, when he had gone to work at the university for the first time, opened it — he counted, in a small careful embarrassed way — nineteen times during the ninety minutes he had been in the flat between waking and leaving, and had, on returning at seven in the evening, opened it four more times before dinner.

He had, on the Monday evening, understood that he was in some trouble.

He had, that Monday evening, done something practical. He had, at eight, gone down to the bakery on the ground floor of the building and had, in his careful Portuguese, asked the small tired woman behind the counter — who was, he had gathered, the wife of the baker and part-owner of the building — whether she knew who had lived in the second-floor flat before him.

The woman, whose name was Dona Fátima, had looked at him for a moment.

She had said: *the second floor.*

He had said: *yes. My flat.*

She had said: *it has been empty for a long time.*

He had said: *how long?*

She had said: *I do not know exactly. Some years. It was renovated last year. Before that — I do not know.*

He had said: *who lived there before the renovation?*

She had said: *before the renovation. Yes. Um homem. A man. He was — he was there for many years. Since I was a girl, I think. He was very old at the end.*

He had said: *do you know his name?*

She had said: *Senhor Cardoso. I do not remember his first name.*

He had said: *what — what did he do?*

She had said: *he was a mathematician, I think. He worked at the university. He had — he had, my mother used to say, been a great mathematician when he was young. When he was old he — he stayed in the flat. He did not come down much. He had, I remember, a woman who came in to bring him his groceries once a week. Sara. Or Susana. I do not remember.*

He had said: *when did he die?*

She had said: *four or five years ago. Perhaps six. I would have to look.*

He had said: *did he — did he die in the flat?*

Dona Fátima had looked at him.

She had said: *yes. He was found by Susana. She came on the Tuesday and she — she found him.*

He had said: *where.*

Dona Fátima had said: *in the bedroom, I think. In his bed. It was — it was not — he was very old. It was expected. It was not a tragedy in that sense.*

He had said: *did he — did he ever mention, do you know, anything unusual about the flat?*

Dona Fátima had looked at him more carefully.

She had said: *what do you mean.*

He had said: *anything strange. Anything he — anything he told you about the flat, or the walls, or —*

Dona Fátima had said, and her face had changed: *anything about the door?*

He had, in the small quiet of the bakery at eight in the evening, felt his shoulders drop slightly.

He had said: *yes.*

She had said: *there is a door in the hallway.*

He had said: *yes.*

She had said, and had looked past him, at the small closed shutters of the bakery, and had, in the way of a woman remembering something she had not thought about in years: *he used to talk about it. Toward the end. He used to say — he used to say strange things about it. That it was — he used to say, sometimes, that it was where the — where the *other one* went.*

Mateus had said: *the other one.*

Dona Fátima had said: *he used to say that. My mother — my mother would take him a plate of something, on Fridays, sometimes — she used to talk to him. He used to say to her, when he was very old, that his brother was in the flat with him. That his brother had been there, in the small back room, for a long time. My mother thought — my mother thought he was, you understand, confused. He had no brother. No brother that anyone knew. He was an only child. But he used to say it. Toward the end.*

She had said: *he was old. He was over ninety when he died.*

Mateus had said, more quietly: *and the door was there when he was alive.*

Dona Fátima had said: *the door has always been there. So far as I know. I do not — I have never been in the flat myself. But my brother, who did the renovation last year — he told me they left the small back room as it was. They had wanted, at first, to open the wall between the bathroom and the bedroom and make it into a proper walk-in wardrobe. But when they measured, they had — the room did not fit. It was — it was more space than there was in the building. They could not, my brother said, make it work in the plans. So they left it alone. They painted it. They left the door on it.*

She had, at this, given a small tight polite smile.

She had said: *anyway. It is a small extra room. Some flats have them. In this old part of the city.*

Mateus had said, quietly: *yes.*

He had said: *thank you, Dona Fátima.*

He had gone upstairs.

—

He had, in his flat, sat on the sofa for a long time.

He had thought about Cardoso.

He had, in the small careful way of a young academic, opened his laptop and had done a small search. He had found, in the university's public records, a Cardoso — Bento Cardoso, professor of mathematics, employed from 1957 to 1999, emeritus until his death in 2020. He had found two published papers by Cardoso from the sixties, on topics in point-set topology. He had found a small note in the departmental newsletter from 2020 announcing Cardoso's death and listing him as *distinguished emeritus, formerly of the topology group, aged 96.*

He had, in the sitting room, sat with this information.

He had thought about the topology group.

He had thought about the specific field of point-set topology — the study of the properties of sets under continuous deformation, the study of what happened to spaces when they were bent, folded, stretched, without being cut or torn. He had, at university, taken one course in it. He had, at the time, found it a strange discipline — a discipline in which one dealt with objects that were not, in any ordinary sense, physical, and which one described using rigorous language that had, if one was not careful, the peculiar property of allowing one to describe things that were not, in ordinary space, describable.

He had, sitting on the sofa, thought about the small back room.

He had thought about the fact that the room had, when he had measured it, been half a meter deeper than the building had space for.

He had thought about the fact that Cardoso had, apparently, kept a brother in the room.

He had thought, and this thought had come with a small careful chill: *he did not keep the brother. The brother was there. And Cardoso was, in some way I do not want to think about too closely, the one who had learned to see him.*

He had gotten up.

He had walked to the hallway.

He had opened the third door.

The small room had been empty.

He had stood in the doorway for a long time.

He had, at last, said aloud, in the small quiet voice one used for such things:

*Are you here.*

There had been no answer.

There had, however, been a small change in the room. The specific quality of the small quiet in the room had, at his question, altered slightly — had, he thought, *attended.* It had been, before his question, a specific ordinary quiet. It had become, after his question, a specific *listening* quiet.

He had, in the small careful way of a man who had spent thirty-one years being polite in unfamiliar rooms, said: *hello.*

There had been no answer.

There had been, again, only the small change in the quality of the attention in the room. It had not moved. It had not made a sound. It had, so far as he could tell, remained where it had always been. But it had, now, been attending to him.

He had closed the door.

He had gone back to the sitting room.

He had sat on the sofa.

He had, for the first time since he had moved to Porto, opened his phone and had scrolled, without particular purpose, through the small archive of messages from his ex-girlfriend Ana in Lisbon, whom he had not spoken to in eleven months, and had, without sending anything, closed the phone.

He had thought: *I could move.*

He had thought: *I could go tomorrow. I could send an email to the agent. I could pay the small penalty for breaking the lease. I could find another apartment.*

He had thought, with the specific quiet honesty he had cultivated in his adult life: *I am not going to.*

He had thought about why.

He had thought about it for a long time.

He had understood, at last — sitting on his own sofa in his own small living room in his own small flat in Porto on a Monday evening in October — that he was not going to move because the small back room had, in the specific way it had attended to him, made him feel less alone.

He had, in the first week of his new job in a new city where he did not yet have friends, come home to a flat that had, in some small way he did not entirely understand, been waiting for him.

He had thought: *this is not what a rational person thinks.*

He had thought: *this is exactly the kind of thinking Cardoso had.*

He had thought, and this thought had come with the specific small clarity of an unwelcome recognition: *Cardoso was a rational person for the whole of his career. He wrote papers on point-set topology. He was, until he was very old, entirely competent. And at some point, in this flat, he began to feel less alone. And that felt like a gift.*

He had thought: *this is what the door is for. It is not, in itself, a horror. It is a *company* that the building offers to a certain kind of tenant.*

He had thought: *I am the certain kind of tenant.*

He had thought, and this thought had had the specific small chill of a full understanding: *the door was not put here by anyone. The room was not built. The building did not make it. It is not a feature of the building. It is a feature of the tenant. It appears when the tenant needs it. Cardoso needed it. I need it. When I am gone, whoever comes next may not need it, and the door will not be there for them, and the flat will be one bedroom and one bathroom and one kitchen and one sitting room, as the plan says.*

He had thought: *the building matches itself to who lives in it. It is a small courtesy the building performs.*

He had sat with this for a very long time.

He had gone, at last, to bed.

He had, that night, not opened the door again.

chapters.title: Company
chapters.body:
He kept the flat.

He had, over the following three months, arranged his life around it. He had gone to work every morning at the university, and had done, in his small careful way, the work he had been hired to do. He had made a small number of friends among the other postdocs. He had, on Friday evenings, gone with them to the small bars along Rua Galeria de Paris and had drunk moderate amounts of beer and had walked home along the Ribeira in the specific pleasant tiredness of a young academic making a life for himself.

He had, in those three months, opened the third door many hundreds of times.

He had, at first, opened it only in the evenings. He had, in the second week, begun to open it in the mornings as well. He had, by the fourth week, been opening it whenever he passed through the hallway — an unconscious habit, in the way one touched the corner of a table or ran one's hand along a bannister. He had, by the eighth week, been going into the small room for extended periods. He had, on a Sunday afternoon in early December, sat on the floor of the small room for perhaps two hours, reading a book he had bought that morning, with the door closed behind him and the small radiator ticking beside him and the specific pale winter light of Porto coming in through the high narrow window.

He had, throughout those hours, felt the small quiet presence in the room with him. It had not spoken. It had not moved. It had simply been, in the small careful way of a person sitting in the corner of a room while another read, present.

He had, on that Sunday evening, understood that the presence had begun, over the course of the last three months, to have a *character.*

He had not been able to say what the character was.

He had been able to say only that the presence was, in some way he could not entirely describe, *particular.* It was not a generic presence. It was not the presence of just anyone. It was, so far as he could tell in his small careful attention to it, a specific person. It had preferences. It preferred the small room, but had, over the last three weeks, begun sometimes to be in the sitting room with him when he sat there in the evenings. It preferred the winter light to the summer light. It preferred, he had gathered, quiet reading to any louder activity. It preferred, above all, that he not attempt to look at it directly.

He had, in the eighth week, tried once to look at it directly.

He had done this in the small back room, in the specific soft light of a December afternoon. He had, standing in the middle of the room, turned suddenly toward the corner where he had, over the last hour, felt the presence to be strongest.

The presence had not been there.

It had, at the moment he had turned, moved. He had felt the small displacement of it — the specific sensation of an attention shifting from one corner of the room to the opposite one, so as to remain behind him. He had turned again. It had, again, moved. He had, standing in the middle of the small room, turned slowly in a full circle, and had felt the presence adjust itself throughout the circle to remain always at his back.

He had, at last, stopped.

He had said, quietly, into the room: *I am sorry.*

The presence had, at his apology, settled. It had, he thought, forgiven him. It had returned to its ordinary position in what he had come to think of as its favorite corner — the small corner near the radiator.

He had understood, at that moment, that the presence would not be looked at.

He had understood, further, that this was, in the small careful arrangement of things, appropriate. He was the *tenant*. He was the person whom the flat had, in its own small way, decided to accommodate. The presence was — he had come, over the weeks, to think of it this way — the presence was the *host*. It was there before him. It had been there, so far as he could tell, before Cardoso. It would be there after him. It permitted him to be in the room. It permitted him to sit on its floor. It permitted him to feel it. But it did not permit him to see it, because to see it would have been to place it in some category of ordinary things, and it was not, so far as he could tell, an ordinary thing.

He had, from that Sunday afternoon onward, not tried to see it.

—

In February he received an email from his mother.

His mother had lived, for the whole of Mateus's life, in a small town outside Coimbra. She had, in the two years since his father had died, been living alone in the small house where Mateus had grown up. She had, in the email, asked him whether he would come home for the small feast day of São Vicente at the end of the month, as he had done every year of his adult life.

He had, sitting at his kitchen table in Porto with his second coffee of the morning, considered the email.

He had considered the small five-hour drive to Coimbra. He had considered the small crowded house of his aunts and cousins. He had considered the specific small tiredness of a weekend of family that would leave him, on the Sunday evening returning to Porto, exhausted in the specific way only family could produce.

He had considered the small back room.

He had considered the fact that if he went to Coimbra, he would be away from the small back room for perhaps forty-eight hours.

He had, in the specific small careful way he had learned to notice things about himself, understood that this consideration had come to him as an *objection.* He had, in some part of himself that he had not consulted, been reluctant to leave the flat for forty-eight hours.

He had put down his coffee.

He had sat at the kitchen table for a long moment.

He had understood, at that moment, that he was no longer entirely free.

He had thought about Cardoso. He had thought about the small tired woman who had brought Cardoso his groceries once a week, and about the fact that Cardoso, in his last years, had not come down from the flat. He had thought about the small progression by which a man could, over decades, arrange his life first around a small comfort and then around a small necessity and finally around the specific absence of any external demand that would take him from what had become, over that time, the entire content of his life.

He had thought: *this is how it happens.*

He had thought: *this is how Cardoso became the sort of man who could, at the end, only speak to his brother in the small back room. He had, over years, gradually stopped going down.*

He had, at that thought, felt a small sharp fear.

He had, for the first time in three months, felt a small sharp fear about the small back room.

—

He had, that evening, opened the door.

He had done it deliberately. He had, throughout the day at the university, thought carefully about what he was going to say. He had, on the walk home, rehearsed it. He had, in the flat, taken off his coat, and had walked directly to the third door, and had opened it.

The small room had been there. The presence had been in its corner.

He had said, standing in the doorway: *I am going to my mother's for the weekend.*

There had been the small quality of attention.

He had said: *I want to tell you before I go. So that you know I am coming back.*

The presence had, at this, done something it had not done before. It had, in a small definite way, *moved.* It had shifted from its ordinary corner to a position closer to the door — closer to Mateus himself. It had, in that shift, made itself, for the first time, slightly more insistent than it had ever been.

Mateus had felt the shift.

He had, for a long moment, been quiet.

He had said, then, quietly: *I am going.*

The presence had not moved back to its corner.

It had, so far as Mateus could tell, remained near the door.

He had said, more firmly: *I am going. I will come back on Sunday.*

The presence had not moved.

He had, in the small quiet of the room, understood something.

He had understood that the presence had been, until this evening, accommodating him. It had been, over the last three months, a small careful host, permitting him to come and go, permitting him to be with it in the small back room as he chose. It had made no demands. It had, so far as he could tell, wanted nothing.

The moment he had told it he was going to leave for a weekend — the moment he had asserted, in effect, an ordinary life outside the flat — the presence had made a demand.

The demand had been: *do not go.*

The demand had not been in words. It had been in the specific weight of the presence near the door. It had been in the small definite way the presence had, for the first time, made itself felt as an *interest* rather than a *company.* It had been, above all, in the specific small quality of the attention that had, since he had made his declaration, sharpened.

Mateus had understood, standing at the door of the small back room on a Wednesday evening in February, that the presence had not, until that moment, cared whether he stayed or went, because it had not, until that moment, considered that he might not stay.

It cared now.

It would, from now on, always care.

He had closed the door.

—

He had gone to Coimbra.

He had, on the Friday morning, packed a small bag. He had, on the Friday afternoon, driven down. He had, over the weekend, seen his mother and his aunts and his cousins. He had eaten the small meals and had drunk the small wines and had, in the specific way of a returning son, been asked the specific questions about his new job and his new city and his new life. He had, in his answers, mentioned that Porto was good, that he liked his flat, that his work was going well.

He had not mentioned the door.

He had, on the Sunday afternoon, said goodbye to his mother, who had, at the front door, held him a moment longer than usual and had said, in her small careful way: *my boy. You look tired.*

He had said: *I am fine.*

She had said: *you look tired. In a way I have not seen before. Are you sleeping?*

He had said: *I am sleeping.*

She had said: *are you eating.*

He had said: *I am eating.*

She had, at last, let him go.

He had driven back to Porto in the small pale Sunday evening. He had, on arrival, parked the car and had gone into the building and had climbed the stairs to the second floor, and had, in the specific small pleasant tiredness of a man returning to his own home, unlocked his door.

He had, on entering the hallway, seen that the third door was open.

He had not left it open. He had, on the Friday morning, closed it, deliberately, as the last thing he had done before leaving the flat. He had checked it. He had, in his small careful way, made sure it was closed.

It was, now, open.

He had, standing in the hallway with his bag in his hand, felt, for the first time since he had moved into the flat, actually afraid.

He had walked to the door.

He had, without going in, looked into the small room.

The small room had been, as it had always been, empty.

But there had been, in the corner near the radiator, a small object on the floor.

He had, hesitantly, gone in.

He had picked up the small object.

It had been an old photograph. It had been a small black-and-white photograph, perhaps five by seven centimeters, of the specific pale yellow tone of a photograph from the nineteen-fifties. It had shown two boys, perhaps eight and ten years old, standing together in a small garden in what looked like southern Portugal in summer, in short trousers and open shirts, both smiling for the camera.

He had turned the photograph over.

On the back, in a small careful hand that he had, from some record he had once seen of Cardoso's handwriting during his university search, thought he recognized, had been written:

*Bento e Miguel, verão 1955.*

*Bento and Miguel, summer 1955.*

Mateus had, for a very long moment, held the photograph.

He had understood, holding it, that Cardoso had left it there.

He had understood, further, that this was a small message from the small back room. The presence had, in his absence, produced, from wherever such things were kept, a photograph of the specific person he had begun to suspect it might be. A specific photograph. A specific brother. A specific summer. Miguel, whom the public records had not known about, who had, if the photograph was to be believed, existed at least until the summer of 1955, and had then, in some small way that was no longer part of the family's public knowledge, ceased.

Mateus had understood that the small back room had been Miguel's room.

He had understood, further, that Miguel had been in the room, in some form, since 1955 or thereabouts. Cardoso, moving into the flat at some later date, had been the tenant who had, in his own way, learned to feel him. Cardoso had, over the course of a life, come to keep him company. Cardoso had, at the end, spoken to him.

Mateus was, now, the next tenant.

The presence had, by leaving the photograph, told him whose company he was keeping.

He had, for a very long time, stood in the small back room with the photograph in his hand.

He had, at last, put the photograph in his pocket.

He had, quietly, said aloud: *hello, Miguel.*

The presence had, at the name, settled. It had, in the small definite way of a small child being addressed by name, become quieter and more content. It had, over the following minute, returned to its ordinary corner. It had gone back to being the small careful company he had known.

Mateus had, at that moment, understood the whole shape of it.

He had understood that he was going to spend the rest of his adult life in this flat. He had understood that he would not, at any point in that life, be able to leave for more than a few days. He had understood that he would, over time, come to arrange his life around Miguel — around a small child who had died in Portugal in 1955 and who had, for reasons no one alive now knew, become attached to a specific small room in a specific building in Porto, and had, over seventy years, kept the small room ready for whoever would come to keep him.

He had understood that he was, now, the one who was keeping him.

He had understood that if he did not, in some future decade, arrange for another tenant to be ready to take over — the way Cardoso, in some form, had prepared the room for the one who would come after him — Miguel would, when Mateus died, be alone again.

He had understood, closing the door of the small room, that he did not, in the specific quiet honest way of a man alone in his own hallway on a Sunday evening, mind.

He had known, closing the door, that this was Cardoso's exact thought at some earlier point in his career.

He had gone into the sitting room.

He had, on the small shelf above the small writing desk, placed the photograph of Bento and Miguel in the summer of 1955.

He had, from then on, kept it there.

He had, in due course, gotten used to it.

He had, in due course, stopped noticing that his life had, in every small important way, been arranged around the small back room and its small quiet company.

He had, in due course, become the sort of man who did not go down often.

He had lived to seventy-two. He had, in the last decade of his life, not left the flat. A woman had come, once a week, to bring him his groceries. She had, at the end, found him in his bed on a Tuesday morning.

The flat had been sold in the following year. It had been renovated. Its plans had been redrawn. The new plans had, according to the small tired real estate agent, shown one bedroom and one bathroom and one kitchen and one sitting room.

The new tenant, a young woman who had, that year, moved to Porto for a job at the university, had discovered the third door on her first evening.

She had, standing in the hallway, put her hand on the handle.

She had turned it.

It had opened.
